newsitem.title: FRANCE: Jospin seen tough on French 1998 spending.
newsitem.headline: Jospin seen tough on French 1998 spending.

text.p: French Prime Minister Lionel Jospin was putting the finishing touches on Friday to ministry spending levels for next year and was expected to settle on a package which could constitute the smallest rise in expenditure in a decade.
"We have had two messages which look pretty rigorous -- the aim for a three percent public deficit in 1998 and the 1.2 percent (rise in ministry) spending," said UBS economist Erick Muller.
"If that happens it would be the smallest rise since 1987. It's never been less than two percent since 1987 even if the 1997 budget bill from (former prime minister Alain) Juppe had aimed for lower."
Government sources have said the aim is to keep the spending rise to less than two percent and one newspaper said on Friday Jospin could even push for a cap of 1.2 percent.

The focus of Jospin's work on Thursday and Friday has been to ensure that the spending allocation is in line with a commitment to limit France's public deficit to three percent of gross domestic product in 1998 in preparation for European monetary union, while rebalancing spending according to new priorities.

The top priority is the employment ministry headed by Jospin's second-in-command, Martine Aubry -- who is in charge of enacting a promise by the new Socialist-led government to create 350,000 jobs for the young in the public sector over the next few years.

Jospin has said this plan, requiring an estimated 10 billion francs in state support next year, will not require new spending and that much of the funding can come from a reorganisation of the already extensive state funds dedicated to helping employment.

Other priority ministries are education, culture and justice, while the defence ministry is in the firing line. Jospin was meeting Education Minister Calude Allegre on Friday as well as Culture Minister Catherine Trautmann and Justice Minister Elizabeth Guigou, each of them separately.
Consultations were also concentrating on the biggest budget ministries, the education, defence and interior ministries, sources said.

Each ministry will receive its 1998 spending allocation letter around August 12 and government officials say there is no plan to reveal the result of Jospin's deliberations while the rest of the budget bill is being prepared for presentation to the cabinet on September 24.
"But all this is without knowing the revenues side (of the budget equation)," said one source.
The toughest part of the 1998 budget has yet to come.

Jospin's government, which took over in early June after ousting the previous centre-right coalition, will turn its attention in the latter part of August to the revenue side of next year's budget mathematics.
The big question, economists say, is whether it can secure higher non-fiscal receipts and the extent to which the government can rely on improved economic growth to boost tax revenues.

The previous government had forecast minimum 2.3 percent growth in 1997 GDP and growth of 2.8 percent in 1998. Economic indicators so far this year have been relatively inconclusive on the timing and strength of a pick-up in the economy.
